nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

flashcards.front: What is a landing zone?
flashcards.back: A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

nodes.title: Order the Azure scope hierarchy

data.scenario: Arrange the four Azure management scopes from broadest (top) to narrowest — the way governance and RBAC inheritance flows.

nodes.explanation: Azure organizes resources top-down: management groups contain subscriptions, subscriptions contain resource groups, and resource groups contain resources. Azure Policy and RBAC assigned higher up are inherited downward.

nodes.title: Azure AI Services (AZ-900): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Azure AI Services (formerly Cognitive Services) provide pre-built AI capabilities accessible via REST APIs — no ML training required. AZ-900 tests which service to use for a given scenario: vision, language, speech, or decision. Azure Machine Learning Studio is tested separately as the platform for building and deploying custom ML models.

flashcards.front: Azure AI Services categories — name the four pillars and a capability from each.
flashcards.back: Vision: Computer Vision (image tagging, OCR), Custom Vision (custom image classifiers), Face API (detection, verification). Language: Azure AI Language (sentiment, NER, key phrases), Translator (text translation), LUIS (intent + entity extraction). Speech: Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech, Speaker Recognition. Decision: Personalizer (RL-based recommendations), Content Moderator, Anomaly Detector.

flashcards.front: Azure Machine Learning Studio — what are its two authoring surfaces?
flashcards.back: Designer: drag-and-drop visual pipeline for users who prefer not to write code — connect dataset, transform, and model modules to build training pipelines. Notebooks: Jupyter-compatible environment for Python/R code; integrates with Azure ML SDK. Both surfaces produce the same underlying AzureML Pipelines and compute resources; the choice is workflow preference, not capability.

flashcards.front: What are the six principles of Microsoft Responsible AI?
flashcards.back: Fairness (systems treat all people equitably), Reliability & Safety (consistent performance, safe failure modes), Privacy & Security (data protection), Inclusiveness (benefits everyone, accessible), Transparency (understandable decisions), Accountability (humans remain responsible for outcomes). The AZ-900 exam expects you to name all six and recognize which principle a given scenario violates.

flashcards.front: Azure OpenAI Service vs standard Azure AI Language — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Azure AI Language: lightweight, task-specific NLP (sentiment, key phrase, NER, translation) — fast, cheap, no prompt engineering. Azure OpenAI: access to GPT-4, GPT-3.5, DALL-E via Azure's compliant infrastructure — use when you need open-ended generation, summarization, code completion, or RAG patterns. OpenAI service requires access approval and is significantly more expensive per call.

questions.q: A dev team needs READY-TO-USE AI APIs across vision (image classification, OCR), language (text analytics, translation), speech (TTS, STT), and decision (anomaly, content moderator). They want REST endpoints, no model training. Which Azure family?
choices: Azure Data Lake Storage (hierarchical object store for analytics workloads)
Azure Cognitive Services (now branded Azure AI Services for pre-trained APIs)
Azure SQL Database (managed Microsoft SQL Server engine for relational data)
Microsoft Sentinel (cloud-native SIEM + SOAR for security operations centres)
questions.explanation: Azure Cognitive Services (rebranded Azure AI Services) is the family of pre-trained REST AI APIs across Vision, Language, Speech, and Decision — no model training required by the consumer. Azure Data Lake Storage is hierarchical object storage for analytics, not AI APIs. Azure SQL Database is a managed relational engine. Microsoft Sentinel is a SIEM / SOAR for security operations, not a general-purpose AI API family.

questions.q: A data-science team wants to TRAIN, deploy, and manage CUSTOM ML models on Azure: notebook environment, distributed training, AutoML, MLOps pipelines, model registry, deployment endpoints. Which Azure service?
questions.explanation: Azure Machine Learning is the end-to-end platform for training, deploying, and operating custom ML models: notebooks, distributed compute, AutoML, MLOps pipelines, model registry, and real-time/batch inference endpoints. Power BI is for BI dashboards and reports, not custom model training. Azure Bot Service builds conversational bots, not arbitrary custom ML models. Cognitive Services provides pre-built AI APIs that you call rather than custom models you train.

questions.q: A team wants a managed full-text + AI-enrichment search service: (a) crawl S3 / Azure Blob / DBs / Cosmos for content, (b) auto-index, (c) optional skillset of OCR + entity recognition + translation + sentiment, (d) REST + SDK query. Which Azure service?
questions.explanation: Azure Cognitive Search (Azure AI Search) is the managed enterprise search service with indexers for Blob, ADLS, Cosmos, SQL, and external sources, plus AI-enrichment skillsets (OCR, entity recognition, translation, sentiment) and REST/SDK query. Log Analytics queries operational telemetry with KQL, not arbitrary content. SQL full-text indexes work only inside a SQL database, not across mixed sources. Bing Search APIs query the public web index, not enterprise content.

questions.q: A team wants to build a chatbot that integrates with Microsoft Teams, Slack, web chat, and Telegram, with natural-language understanding via the Language service. Which Azure offering provides the SDK + channel connectors + bot management?
questions.explanation: Azure Bot Service provides the Bot Framework SDK, channel connectors (Teams, Slack, web chat, Telegram, etc.), and managed bot hosting; it integrates with Azure AI Language for NLU. Azure Sphere is a hardware-software IoT security platform, not chatbots. IoT Hub is a device gateway. Power Automate orchestrates workflows; it can call bots but is not the bot SDK + channel platform.

questions.q: An app dev team wants 'high-level' purpose-built AI APIs: extract structured data from invoices (Form Recognizer), detect anomalies in time-series (Metrics Advisor), summarise long documents — without training their own ML models. Which Azure AI family?
questions.explanation: Azure Applied AI Services are higher-level, scenario-specific services (Form Recognizer/Document Intelligence, Metrics Advisor, Immersive Reader, etc.) built on top of Cognitive Services for specific business problems. Azure OpenAI Service hosts OpenAI foundation models for general-purpose generation, not the scenario-specific Applied family. Azure ML Studio is for custom model training. Bot Service builds chatbots and is much narrower than the Applied AI portfolio.

questions.q: A cloud administrator wants an AI-powered assistant integrated directly into the Azure portal to help design architectures, write CLI commands, query resource health, and troubleshoot issues using natural language. Which Microsoft service provides this capability?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Copilot in Azure is the AI assistant embedded in the Azure portal that helps users design, operate, optimise, and troubleshoot Azure resources via natural-language prompts. Azure Monitor Insights are scoped solutions (VM Insights, Container Insights) for monitoring telemetry, not a conversational assistant. Advisor surfaces rule-based recommendations but no natural-language chat. Azure Resource Explorer is a read-only ARM-API browser, not an AI assistant.

questions.q: A team needs to deploy GPT-4 and other OpenAI models in Azure with enterprise features such as private networking, content filtering, responsible AI controls, and regional data residency. Which Azure service should they use?
questions.explanation: Azure OpenAI Service (now part of Azure AI Foundry) provides managed access to OpenAI models (GPT-4, GPT-4o, DALL-E, Whisper, embeddings) with Azure enterprise controls: private endpoints, content filters, customer-managed keys, and regional deployments. Azure Bot Service orchestrates conversational bots and can call OpenAI but is not the model-hosting service. Azure ML Studio is for training/deploying your own custom models. Azure Cognitive Search powers retrieval, often paired with OpenAI in RAG patterns, but is not the GPT model host.

nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

flashcards.front: What is autoscaling?
flashcards.back: A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.

flashcards.front: Reserved / committed-use vs on-demand pricing.
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

questions.q: A team needs to run Python event-driven code triggered by Blob uploads, HTTP requests, and a 5-min timer — billed per execution (not per VM hour), auto-scaled, with no VM or container to manage. Which Azure service?
questions.explanation: Azure Functions is the serverless, event-driven compute service: it runs code in response to triggers (Blob, HTTP, timer, queue) and on the Consumption plan is billed per execution and per GB-second of memory. Azure Container Instances is serverless containers billed per second of vCPU/memory, not per execution. Azure VMs are IaaS billed per VM-hour. Azure App Service is PaaS for long-running web apps and APIs, billed by App Service Plan size rather than per execution.

questions.q: A web tier behind an Azure Load Balancer experiences predictable daytime peaks. The team wants identical VM instances that AUTOMATICALLY add/remove based on CPU or schedule, using a shared image, with rolling-upgrade support. Which Azure compute construct?
choices: Standalone Azure VMs in an Availability Set
Azure Functions on the Consumption plan
questions.explanation: Azure VM Scale Sets deploy and manage a group of identical, load-balanced VMs that automatically scale in and out based on metrics or schedule, and support rolling image upgrades. Standalone VMs in an Availability Set provide HA distribution but no built-in autoscale across the fleet. AKS node pools are for Kubernetes worker nodes, not plain VMs behind a Load Balancer. Azure Functions is serverless event-driven compute, not a VM-based scale construct.

questions.q: A team wants to deploy a Node.js / .NET / Python web app to Azure WITHOUT managing OS / runtime / patching / scaling. Azure provides a managed PaaS that handles the runtime, SSL, autoscale, custom domains, deployment slots, and CI/CD from GitHub. Which Azure service?
questions.explanation: Azure App Service is a managed PaaS that hosts web apps and APIs in .NET, Node.js, Python, Java, PHP, or containers, handling OS patching, runtime, autoscale, TLS, custom domains, slots, and CI/CD from GitHub or Azure DevOps. Azure VMs are IaaS where the customer manages OS and runtime. AKS is managed Kubernetes — still requires container expertise. Azure Container Registry only stores container images; it doesn't run web apps.

questions.q: A Java team runs 25 Spring Boot microservices. They want a managed PaaS that natively understands Spring Boot: service discovery, config server, blue/green deployment, distributed tracing, autoscale, monitoring — without operating any infrastructure. Which Azure service?
questions.explanation: Azure Spring Apps (developed jointly with VMware/Broadcom) is the managed PaaS that natively supports Spring Boot with Eureka-style discovery, Config Server, blue/green slots, distributed tracing, and autoscale. Azure Container Apps is a general serverless container platform without Spring-specific service discovery and config-server primitives. Azure App Service can run Spring Boot JARs as generic Java apps but lacks Spring's native service-discovery integrations. Service Fabric is Microsoft's own microservices orchestrator, not a Spring-specific runtime.

questions.q: Two HA constructs in Azure: (A) groups VMs within the SAME datacentre but across distinct fault and update domains — protects from rack-level outages. (B) groups VMs across DIFFERENT physically-isolated facilities with independent power and network — protects from facility-level outages. Which mapping?
choices: Availability Sets and Availability Zones provide identical protection at the same SLA
Availability Sets span multiple Azure regions for cross-region redundancy
Availability Set = fault/update domains in one datacentre; Zone = isolated datacentres in a region
Availability Zones were the original construct and predate Availability Sets in Azure
questions.explanation: Availability Sets group VMs across fault and update domains inside a single datacentre (99.95% SLA, rack-level protection). Availability Zones place VMs across physically isolated datacentres inside one region with independent power, cooling, and network (99.99% SLA, facility-level protection). The two are not identical and carry different SLAs. Sets are confined to one datacentre, not multiple regions. Sets are the older construct; Zones were introduced later — the last option reverses that history.

questions.q: A research team needs to run thousands of parallel compute jobs (Monte-Carlo, batch rendering, genomics) with auto-scaled VM pools, queue-of-tasks dispatch, support for low-priority spot nodes, and result aggregation. Which Azure service?
questions.explanation: Azure Batch provisions and scales pools of VMs, schedules large numbers of parallel tasks, supports low-priority/spot nodes for cost savings, and aggregates output — the canonical HPC/batch service. Data Factory orchestrates data-engineering pipelines, not generic parallel compute. Service Bus is a messaging broker, not a compute scheduler. SQL Database elastic jobs run T-SQL across many databases; they are not a general HPC compute platform.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

nodes.title: Identity providers and federation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Modern identity is centralized — one identity provider issues tokens that every application trusts. SAML and OIDC are the two interop standards. Federation means trusting another organization's identity provider for cross-org access.

flashcards.front: SAML vs OIDC — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: SAML: XML, browser-redirect-heavy, used for enterprise SSO into web apps. OIDC (on top of OAuth 2.0): JSON, mobile- and SPA-friendly, the modern default. New integrations should use OIDC; existing SAML works fine, no urgent reason to migrate.

flashcards.front: What's an IdP vs an SP (service provider)?
flashcards.back: Identity Provider: where users actually authenticate (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, Auth0). Service Provider: the app the user is trying to use (Slack, Salesforce, your custom app). The IdP issues a signed token; the SP trusts the IdP's signature and reads the user's identity from the token.

flashcards.front: MFA — why is push notification preferred over SMS?
flashcards.back: SMS is sniffable (SS7 attacks) and SIM-swappable. Push (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator, OS-level biometric) is bound to a specific device, requires user interaction, harder to phish. WebAuthn / FIDO2 hardware keys are the gold standard — phishing-resistant by design.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning — what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Instead of pre-creating users in every app, JIT creates the user on first SSO login, hydrated from the IdP's attributes. Onboarding a new hire: add to the IdP group once, every app that supports JIT auto-creates them on first visit. Deprovisioning is the inverse — IdP removes them, apps refuse next login.

questions.q: An organisation's M365 users sign in with email + password to access SharePoint, Teams, Outlook, AND third-party SaaS apps via SAML/OIDC federation. The user directory + MFA + SSO + B2B Guest invites all live in one Microsoft cloud product. Which one?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's cloud identity platform: it provides authentication for M365 and Azure, SAML/OIDC SSO to third-party SaaS, MFA, and B2B guest invitations. On-premises AD DS is the on-prem directory service that does not natively federate to cloud SaaS without sync. Intune is Microsoft's endpoint management service, not the identity directory. Azure DNS resolves DNS names and has no identity role.

questions.q: A bank's CISO mandates that the SECOND factor of authentication must not be replayable from a stolen password alone. After entering the password, users must complete a SEPARATE verification (push notification, hardware token, biometric). Which security control is this?
choices: Periodic forced password rotation enforced by a domain Group Policy Object
Self-service password reset (SSPR) with email + mobile verification questions
Single sign-on (SSO) reusing one cloud authentication across many SaaS apps
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) combining password with a separate factor
questions.explanation: MFA requires two or more verification factors drawn from different categories — something you know (password), something you have (phone/token), or something you are (biometric) — so a stolen password alone cannot satisfy it. Password rotation is hygiene, not a second factor. SSPR lets a user reset their own password but is not itself an authentication factor used at sign-in. SSO improves convenience by reusing one authentication across apps but does not by itself add a second verification factor.

questions.q: An identity team compares two Entra ID licence editions: FREE (basic user/group management, SSO to popular SaaS apps) vs PREMIUM (Conditional Access, PIM, Identity Protection risk-based policies, dynamic groups, MFA enforcement at policy level). Which is the key Premium feature set?
choices: Conditional Access, Privileged Identity Management, and Identity Protection
Basic user/group management and SSO to popular SaaS gallery apps (Free tier)
MFA enabled only for global administrators via Security Defaults baseline
Self-service password reset limited to cloud-only users without writeback
questions.explanation: Entra ID Premium P1 adds Conditional Access and PIM, with P2 layering Identity Protection risk-based policies, dynamic groups, and policy-level MFA enforcement — the differentiating Premium feature set. Basic user/group management plus SSO to gallery SaaS apps is included in the Free tier. MFA limited to global admins via Security Defaults is also part of Free. Cloud-only SSPR is Free; the Premium differentiator is SSPR with writeback to on-prem AD.

questions.q: Your organization was using 'Azure Active Directory' for identity and access management. You notice Microsoft now refers to it by a new name in the portal and documentation. What is the current official name of this service?
questions.explanation: In 2023, Microsoft rebranded Azure Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID as part of the broader Microsoft Entra product family; capabilities such as tenants, users, groups, Conditional Access, and MFA are unchanged. Azure AD Premium is a former SKU name, not the new service name. Microsoft 365 Identity is not an official product name. Azure Identity Manager is not a real Microsoft product.

nodes.title: Azure pricing models: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Azure pricing combines consumption-based, reservation, and hybrid-benefit models. The AZ-900 exam tests the difference between CapEx and OpEx and how Azure's pricing calculator and TCO calculator help estimate costs.

flashcards.front: CapEx vs OpEx in a cloud context?
flashcards.back: CapEx = upfront hardware purchase (on-premises). OpEx = pay-as-you-go subscription (cloud). Cloud shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx.

flashcards.front: Azure Reservations — how much can they save?
flashcards.back: Commit to 1- or 3-year terms for VMs, databases, or other services; save up to 72% compared to pay-as-you-go rates.

flashcards.front: Azure Hybrid Benefit?
flashcards.back: Use existing on-premises Windows Server or SQL Server licences (with Software Assurance) on Azure VMs to reduce or eliminate the licence cost.

flashcards.front: Azure Pricing Calculator vs TCO Calculator?
flashcards.back: Pricing Calculator: estimate cost of specific Azure services you plan to use. TCO Calculator: compare on-premises infrastructure cost against equivalent Azure deployment.

questions.q: A team commits to running a specific VM size in West Europe 24×7 for 3 years. Microsoft offers a UPFRONT-COMMITMENT pricing tier in exchange for the steady commitment. The published discount cap vs pay-as-you-go is approximately 72%. Which Azure pricing benefit?
choices: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (deeply discounted but interruptible spare capacity)
Azure Hybrid Benefit (re-use of existing Windows/SQL licences for compute discount)
Azure Dev/Test pricing (discounted rates for non-production EA or PAYG Dev/Test)
Reserved VM Instances (1- or 3-year commitment with up to ~72% PAYG discount)
questions.explanation: Reserved VM Instances offer up to roughly 72% savings versus pay-as-you-go in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment to a specific VM size and region. Spot VMs offer discounts on interruptible capacity, not steady reservations. Azure Hybrid Benefit applies existing Windows Server or SQL Server licences to reduce Azure costs but is not the commitment-based discount described. Dev/Test pricing is a discounted rate for non-production workloads under EA or PAYG Dev/Test, not an upfront-commitment reservation.

questions.q: A new Azure customer with no existing Azure spend wants to evaluate the platform for a month. Microsoft offers a free starter that includes $200 of credit for 30 days, free monthly amounts of popular services for 12 months, AND a catalogue of 25+ always-free services. Which offer?
choices: Azure for Students ($100 credit for verified students, no credit card required)
Azure Dev/Test pricing (discounted non-production rates under EA or PAYG Dev/Test)
Azure Free Account ($200 / 30 days, 12-month free tier, 25+ always-free services)
Azure Nonprofit Grant (separate sponsored credit program for qualifying NGOs)
questions.explanation: The Azure Free Account is the standard new-customer offer: $200 credit for 30 days, 12 months free for popular services (e.g., B1S VM, 5 GB Blob), and a permanent catalogue of always-free services. Azure for Students is a separate offer ($100 credit, no card required) limited to verified students. Azure Dev/Test pricing applies a discount to non-production workloads under an EA — not a free trial. Azure Nonprofit grants are a separate program for qualifying NGOs.

questions.q: A finance team commits to a STEADY 3-year workload of a specific VM size in a specific region. In exchange for the upfront commitment, Microsoft offers up to ~72% discount versus pay-as-you-go. The discount applies automatically as the running VMs match the commitment. Which Azure pricing model?
choices: Azure Hybrid Benefit (re-use of existing Windows/SQL licences for compute discount)
Azure Reserved VM Instances (1- or 3-year commitment, up to ~72% off PAYG rates)
Azure Spot Virtual Machines (interruptible capacity at deep discount, no commitment)
Azure Dev/Test pricing (discounted rates for non-production EA or PAYG Dev/Test plans)
questions.explanation: Azure Reserved VM Instances give up to ~72% savings versus pay-as-you-go in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment to a VM size and region; the discount applies automatically when matching VMs run. Azure Hybrid Benefit re-uses existing Windows Server or SQL Server licences to reduce compute cost, but is not the commitment-based reservation. Spot VMs give discounts on interruptible capacity with no steady commitment. Dev/Test pricing applies to non-production EA or PAYG Dev/Test subscriptions, not the VM reservation model.

questions.q: A new Azure customer signs up. The offer they activate gives them $200 in credit usable for 30 days, plus 12 months of free monthly amounts of POPULAR services (e.g., 750h B1S VM, 5GB Blob), plus 25+ services that are ALWAYS free up to a quota. Which offer?
choices: Azure for Students ($100 credit for verified students, no credit card required)
Azure Dev/Test pricing (non-production discount under EA or PAYG Dev/Test plans)

questions.explanation: The Azure Free Account is the standard new-customer offer: $200 credit for 30 days, 12 months free for popular services, and 25+ always-free services. Azure for Students is a separate program with $100 credit and no credit-card requirement, limited to verified students. Dev/Test pricing applies discounts to non-production workloads under an EA, not free credit. An Enterprise Agreement is a large-organisation volume commitment, not a free-trial offer.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
